newsitem.title: NORWAY: Computer theft claims rising, say cargo insurers.
newsitem.headline: Computer theft claims rising, say cargo insurers.

text.p: Thefts of computer parts and memory chips have soared, leaving insurers around the world stuck for a solution to rising claims, a marine insurance industry report said.

Substantial increases in thefts and non-delivery of shipments, mostly from air and overland routes, have been reported by cargo insurance associations around the world to the International Union of Marine Insurers (IUMI), which is meeting in Oslo this week.
The problem stems from high global demand for computers, parts and particularly memory chips, which makes it easy for them to re-enter the production chain.
Insurers are concerned that their high value, compared with the very low recovery from cargo carriers, is leaving them with massive claims bills.
IUMI member associations reported 26 separate incidents last year where the loss was worth more than $200,000, and some went as high as $1.5 million.
Australia reported several losses in the A$50,000-A$100,000 bracket involving computer components stolen during air transport via Taipei and Hong Kong.
Other airports targeted by computer thieves included London Heathrow, Johannesburg International and Amsterdam, the report said.

In an attempt to solve the problem, insurers are encouraging greater use of non-descriptive labelling on packages, coded markings changed regularly to deter thieves from pilfering packages with unknown content and the installation of satellite tracking devices for vehicles carrying such cargoes.
Other suggestions include welding the doors of containers and employing armed guards.
"It really is a problem which shows no signs of abating, and in the U.S. in particular single claims can easily exceed $1 million," one leading air cargo insurer told Reuters.

"It should really be up to the carriers to do more and for exporters to avoid trans-shipment and employ greater secrecy. After encouragement to take preventative action, insurers can do little more than increase deductibles and premiums," he added.
